newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania protesters plan new rallies over lost cash.
newsitem.headline: Albania protesters plan new rallies over lost cash.

text.p: Albania's rejuvenated opposition planned fresh protests on Sunday to demand the dismissal of the right-wing government and a fair deal for investors who lost their life savings in failed pyramid investment schemes.

A week after pitched street battles with police across the country, parties united in a new Forum for Democracy against President Sali Berisha said they would hold demonstrations in the Adriatic port of Durres and the town of Lezhe further north.
Trade unionists led by a veteran of the successful struggle to topple the communist regime in 1990 were organising a rally in Tirana, the capital of Europe's poorest state.

State television, in its main Saturday newscast, made no mention of the proposed protests but it broadcast 20 minutes of appeals from intellectuals, clergymen and ordinary Albanians to prevent a repeat of last week's violence.
"It is not in the Albanian character to resort to violence," music critic Ramadan Sokoli told the television.
"How is this possible in a democracy?" pleaded an elderly woman. "The president is working hard to improve our lives."
Television also showed rallies in two towns backing the government and it reported the killing of three ethnic Albanians by police in Serbia's Kosovo region.

Demonstrators last week set fire to government buildings and offices of Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, mostly in the south of the country once isolated from the world by hardline communist Enver Hoxha.

Virtually every family in Albania had a stake in the pyramid schemes, which promised quick and fabulous returns to a public unfamiliar with the workings of financial markets. Most of the money came from relatives working abroad.

Berisha has pledged that the poorest depositors will be the first to receive compensation, beginning next week, from $300 million frozen by the government in state savings banks. Others, he said, would get government certificates or shares.
A Tirana court has charged five employees of the two main pyramid schemes with embezzlement, the official ATA news agency reported.

The opposition, led by the Socialists, demands the formation of a new government and accuses authorities of intimidation. At least 149 people have been detained and prosecutors say they face up to 15 years in jail if convicted of incitement.

The former head of the Supreme Court, now living in the United States after Berisha sacked him for challenging the jailing of a top government opponent, said the government used pyramid funds to finance its election camaigns and was turning Albania into a police state.
Several people in Tirana said they had lost their savings in the pyramid scheme but shunned violence and regarded Berisha as their last hope for recovering some of their money.
"We invested in the scheme after the Democrats were elected for the second time last year," said one 70-year-old man who, like virtually all those questioned, declined to give his name.
"We were 100 percent sure things would be all right. I have nothing against Berisha. But God help us get our money back."
The Socialists and Democrats have accused each other of using proceeds from pyramid schemes for campaign funding.
Berisha's Democrats won last May's election and have a stranglehold on parliament, boycotted by the opposition. Western observers say the election was marred by serious irregularities.
